name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
description: Low skill can come with poor self-monitoring, leading some people to rate their own competence too highly. In design work the label is safest when used for self-assessment errors, not as a casual insult for disagreement.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to self-assessment UX, creator and education tools, expert/novice workflows, calibration feedback, and onboarding systems that ask users to judge their own skill or readiness.
myth_risk_note: The core phenomenon is empirically supported but genuinely disputed -- this corpus already documents a real statistical-artifact critique, and this pass found a second, independent limitation in reasoning contexts, so the popular conception likely overstates the effect's universality and magnitude.
prevalence_note: One of the most culturally widespread psychology labels in workplace and product discourse, even though it is often used more loosely and more often than the evidence strictly supports.

findings.description: Across 4 studies of humor, grammar, and logic tests, participants scoring in the bottom quartile of actual performance (12th percentile) grossly overestimated their own performance and ability, placing themselves at the 62nd percentile on average; this miscalibration was linked to deficits in metacognitive skill (the capacity to distinguish accuracy from error) rather than to a general self-serving bias alone, since improving participants' actual skill also improved their ability to recognize the limits of their competence.
findings.effect_size: Actual 12th percentile vs. self-estimated 62nd percentile (bottom-quartile performers)
findings.source_title: Unskilled and unaware of it: How difficulties in recognizing one's own incompetence lead to inflated self-assessments
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

findings.description: Using statistically valid tests for the Dunning-Kruger hypothesis (a Glejser heteroscedasticity test and nonlinear/quadratic regression, rather than the traditional quartile-plot comparison that is confounded by the better-than-average effect and regression toward the mean), a sample of 929 general-community participants showed no statistically significant heteroscedasticity and an essentially linear relationship between objectively measured and self-assessed intelligence — contrary to the Dunning-Kruger hypothesis's predicted differential-miscalibration pattern across ability levels. The authors conclude the underlying phenomenon may be real for some skills but its magnitude has likely been substantially overstated by the original quartile-plot method.
findings.source_title: The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact: Valid approaches to testing the hypothesis with individual differences data

applications.title: A software developer's own account of climbing the Dunning-Kruger confidence curve
applications.description: Developer and Built In contributor Aphinya Dechalert describes her own career arc through the Dunning-Kruger effect: early-career overconfidence ('the cocky junior dev'), a subsequent crash in self-assessed competence once she recognized how much she didn't know, and a slow rebuild of genuine confidence through deliberate practice (starting projects from a scoped idea rather than diving into unfamiliar technology first). Framed explicitly around the Dunning-Kruger curve as a lived experience in a technical career, not an abstract psychology lesson.
applications.ethical_note: A self-reflective account of one's own overconfidence and its correction over time, with no persuasive or commercial intent toward others.

applications.title: About 80% of drivers rate themselves as 'above average' -- a mathematical impossibility
applications.description: Surveys have repeatedly found that about 80% of people rate themselves as 'above-average' drivers, a statistic that is mathematically impossible if 'average' is taken literally. This inflated sense of driving ability is linked to real-world consequences: novice drivers with less than six months of experience are eight times more likely to be involved in an accident, in part because overconfidence in their control over the vehicle leads to riskier decisions on the road.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, well-established pattern in self-assessment with genuine public-safety stakes, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no party attempting to manipulate driver behavior here, only a documented mismatch between self-perceived and actual skill with real accident-risk consequences.
